tagline: The train still stops for a wave of a white cloth.
intro: The main line starts at tidewater in Seward and runs about 470 miles north to Fairbanks. Within 48 miles of Seward the Bartlett and Spencer glaciers come into view, and a short spur tunnels through the Chugach Mountains to Whittier. Then it follows Turnagain Arm to Anchorage, which began in 1914 as the railroad's construction camp on Ship Creek and is now the state's largest city.

It is one of the last lines in the country where the train stops wherever a passenger wants on or off. Between Talkeetna and the Hurricane area there are no roads at all, and on the Hurricane Turn a rider boards by waving a large white flag or cloth beside the track.

moments.title: Talkeetna
moments.text: A town that began in 1916 as a railroad district headquarters, where three rivers meet, and now the base for expeditions to Denali.

moments.title: Hurricane Gulch Bridge
moments.text: The train crosses a 918-foot steel arch at Milepost 284, 296 feet above Hurricane Creek, built from both sides at once off an aerial tram strung across the gulch in 1921.

moments.title: Nenana
moments.text: At the north end of the 700-foot bridge over the Tanana, Harding, the first president to visit Alaska, drove the golden spike on July 15, 1923, and died 18 days later.

practical: Passenger trains run year-round between Anchorage and Fairbanks. Service to Seward, Whittier, Talkeetna and Denali is offered in summer.
